claims.text: Wear resistance in HEA protective coatings is primarily governed by maintenance of a stable nanocrystalline, chemically disordered grain-boundary network.
The grain-boundary network impedes dislocation motion under high-stress sliding conditions.
The as-deposited coating has a nanocrystalline microstructure.
The as-deposited coating has a high volume fraction of chemically disordered grain boundaries.
The as-deposited coating is a single-phase solid solution.
Heat treatment will promote grain growth.
Heat treatment will promote partial phase segregation.
Heat-treatment-induced grain growth will reduce the nanocrystalline grain-boundary network.
High configurational entropy intrinsic to HEAs stabilizes a fine, chemically disordered microstructure.
The fine, disordered microstructure acts as a barrier to dislocation motion.
Restricting dislocation motion reduces the initiation and propagation of plastic deformation during wear.
Reducing grain-boundary area through grain growth decreases obstacles to dislocation motion.
The reduction in grain-boundary obstacles increases dislocation mobility and wear rate.
Heat-treated, grain-grown coatings will have significantly higher wear rates than as-deposited nanocrystalline coatings under otherwise identical tests.
Heat-treated, grain-grown coatings may have higher friction coefficients than as-deposited nanocrystalline coatings.
The proposed mechanism should apply to HEA coatings whose compositions favor a single-phase nanocrystalline structure.
Coarse-grained or phase-separated HEA coatings may not show the predicted trend.
The role of the grain-boundary network is supported by general HEA behavior.
The magnitude of the effect may vary with alloy composition and processing history.
Oxide formation or other auxiliary wear mechanisms may also affect wear performance.

contradictions.description: The predicted friction increase is qualified as merely possible, but the falsification rule treats failure to observe a statistically significant friction increase as sufficient to falsify the hypothesis. Unchanged friction therefore conflicts with the stated prediction only weakly and should not independently be decisive if wear rate increases as predicted.
